title: Biblestudy Furnace
subject: Torts
stem:
Daniel was using a six-foot stepladder to clean the furnace in his home before hosting a Bible-study dinner. Daniel broke his arm when he slipped and fell from the ladder. The furnace had no warnings or instructions on how it was to be cleaned.

In Daniel’s suit against the manufacturer of the furnace to recover for his injury, is Daniel likely to prevail?
call: In Daniel’s suit against the manufacturer of the furnace to recover for his injury, is Daniel likely to prevail?

choices.A: No, because the danger of falling from a ladder is obvious.
choices.B: No, because Daniel should have hired a professional to clean the furnace.
choices.C: Yes, because the furnace did not have a ladder attached to it for cleaning purposes.
choices.D: Yes, because the lack of warnings or instructions for how to clean the furnace made the furnace defective.

rightExplanation:
A is correct. The injury came from the ordinary, visible risk of falling from a six-foot stepladder, not from a hidden danger unique to the furnace.

Gold Key: A manufacturer generally does not have to warn about an open and obvious danger. Here, the danger that materialized was falling from a ladder. A warning on the furnace about ordinary ladder balance would not turn the furnace into a defective product merely because the manufacturer omitted it.

Silver Key: Do not let “no warnings” automatically become “defective.” First ask what risk caused the injury. If the risk is an ordinary, obvious outside risk, the warning-defect answer is the trap.

wrongExplanations.B: This choice gives a common-sense scolding answer, not the product-defect reason. The issue is not whether Daniel made the best household decision. The issue is whether the furnace manufacturer had to warn about the risk that injured him. Hiring a professional is not the rule.
wrongExplanations.C: This invents an accessory rule. A furnace manufacturer is not required to attach a ladder merely because a homeowner might use a ladder to clean the furnace. The answer adds a design requirement that the problem does not support.
wrongExplanations.D: This is the dominant trap. It sounds like a real warning-defect answer because warnings and instructions can matter in products liability. But Gold Key: no warning is required for an obvious danger. Silver Key: the injury source is the ladder fall, not a hidden furnace-specific danger. The missing-warning fact is not enough by itself.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: “Should have hired a professional” is common-sense blame language. It does not supply the product-defect rule.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: “Had no ladder attached” fabricates a product-design requirement.

c3.label: CLASH A vs. D
c3.text: A says the risk was obvious. D says the lack of warnings made the product defective.

c3.label: CALL with Gold Key
c3.text: no duty to warn of open and obvious danger. A survives.

studentScript: Cut B as common-sense blame. Cut C as invented ladder requirement. Clash A against D. The harm is a ladder fall. Gold Key: no warning required for obvious danger. Pick A.

A.signal: This answer directly names the risk source: falling from a ladder.
A.lawyer: Correct. A failure-to-warn claim fails where the only risk that materialized was open and obvious rather than a hidden product risk.

B.signal: The answer scolds Daniel for not hiring a professional. That is not a product-defect test.
B.lawyer: Incorrect. The manufacturer wins, but not because routine furnace cleaning legally had to be done by a professional.

C.signal: The answer invents a rule that furnaces must come with ladders.
C.lawyer: Incorrect. A manufacturer is not required to attach a general household ladder to a furnace merely because a ladder might be used for cleaning.

D.signal: This proves only that warnings were absent. It does not answer whether this missing warning mattered for the risk that caused the injury.
D.lawyer: Incorrect. Missing warnings can create a defect, but not for an ordinary obvious risk like falling from a ladder.

goldKeys.statement: A manufacturer generally has no duty to warn about an open and obvious danger; missing warnings matter only when the risk is one users need the manufacturer to disclose.
goldKeys.trigger: Plaintiff is injured by an ordinary outside risk while using a product, and the missing-warning answer says the product is defective.
goldKeys.unlocks: Defeats the warning-defect trap in D.
goldKeys.authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability § 2(c), comment j; Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A, comment j; general MBE products-liability rule.

silverKeys.statement: When a warning answer is fighting an obvious-danger answer, ask what risk actually caused the injury before asking whether a warning was missing.
silverKeys.trigger: One answer says 'obvious danger'; another says 'lack of warnings made the product defective.'
silverKeys.unlocks: A/D fight pair: obvious ladder danger versus warning-defect theory.

remediation.title: Missing Warning Is Not Enough
remediation.signal: Answer says 'no warning, therefore defective' while the injury came from an ordinary visible risk.
remediation.studentMove: Find the risk that caused the harm. Then ask whether the product maker had to disclose that risk.
remediation.tinyRule: No warning required for obvious ordinary dangers.
remediation.trap: Automatically converting missing instructions into product defect.
